a:r.a:t: Ion Channels Can Respond to Cellular Voltage Changes

p:cNvPr.descr: Illustrations of various models of voltage-gated potassium channels. (a) A ribbon structure of a voltage-gated K+ channel. The channel itself is membrane spanning and consists of multicolored vertically oriented helices. The protein consists of red helices, which are concentrated on the left and labeled S1 to S4 from left to right; of blue helices, which are not numbered; of green helices, one of which is labeled K+ at the top; and yellow helices, to the far right side of the protein. One random red helix is found overlapping the green and yellow. This is labeled S6. The helices all fold inward once they cross the membrane to inside the cell and create a small opening in the center of all the helices. (b) Below, a perpendicular plane ribbon model of the K+ channel. The center of the protein consists of a roughly square mass of protein helices, with green helices concentrated at the top left, yellow helices at the top right, red helices at the bottom right, and blue helices at the bottom left. The masses of each color of helices weave over and under one another so that their ends stick out like flower petals. Green sticks out from the upper right side, yellow sticks out from the lower right, red sticks out from the lower left, and blue sticks out from the upper left. The red helices on the lower left are labeled S1-4; S5 and S6 are on the central portion. (c) Upper right. A cylindrical representation of the K+ channel. 2 large irregular pale pink cylinders labeled S1-S3 are placed apart on the cell membrane. Each bonds down to NH3+ and up to a connecting loop. The connecting loop bonds down to 2 thin, dark pink cylinders labeled S4, one on either side; they have + signs all down their length. These are labeled the voltage sensors. These connecting loops then bond up to a mass of pale pink cylinders labeled S5 and S6, one on each side. S5 is a shorter cylinder than S6 and they are each connected to 2 shorter, unlabeled pale pink proteins. The connecting loop emerges at the bottom bonded to COO-. (d) An aerial view of the channel showing its opening and closing. The top is labeled “view from the inside face.” The woven nature of the protein units means that there is a variable-sized pore in its center. The multicolored ribbon helices are still used, with green on top, yellow on the right, red on bottom, and blue on the left, each overlapping with the next. On the left is the open conformation, in which the protein units have moved slightly apart to open the pore all the way through. In the center is a green K+ ion. On the right is the closed conformation, which does not appear different, as there is still a green K+ ion inside. Both proteins are surrounded by a white surface contour material to show the shape of the protein.
